concept.name: Strike price
concept.definition: The price, specified in the option contract, at which the underlying security, futures contract, or commodity will be bought (call) or sold (put) if the option is exercised.
concept.intuition: The strike is the deal price locked in at contract creation: it is the yardstick that decides whether exercising the option is worth anything.
concept.mechanics: Exchanges list standardized series of strikes around the current underlying price. The strike fixes intrinsic value (max(S-K,0) for a call, max(K-S,0) for a put) and moneyness: calls are in-the-money when the underlying trades above the strike, puts when it trades below.
concept.formula: Call intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0); put intrinsic value = max(K - S, 0), where S = underlying price and K = strike price.
concept.failure_modes: Comparing options across different strikes as if the premium alone measures cheapness ignores that the strike determines both payoff and probability of finishing in-the-money.
concept.misconceptions: The strike is not a price target or forecast — it is a contractual term chosen from listed series, and an at-the-money option is not 'fairly priced' by definition.
concept.example: A holder of an OICX July 60 call can buy the underlying stock at $60 per share until expiration; if the stock trades at $68, the call has $8 of intrinsic value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
